name: Sungazing

lead: Sungazing is looking directly at the sun, usually near dawn or dusk, as a spiritual or health practice. In looksmaxxing forums users discuss it for eyesight, mood, skin and lighter eye colour. William Horatio Bates promoted it in the early 20th century as 'sunning' in his eye exercises for myopia.

Proponents say sunlight entering the eyes affects hormones, circadian rhythm and mood, and some believe it changes iris pigment. No published trial has tested vision or appearance benefits. Ophthalmology literature describes a different outcome: high-energy visible and ultraviolet light can damage retinal cells, and the retina has no pain receptors, so injury can go unnoticed.

paras: Practitioners look toward the sun for short periods near sunrise or sunset, as a daily ritual. Some users post about their own experiences, including floaters.

Solar retinopathy typically causes central blind spots, distorted vision and light sensitivity. Many cases recover over weeks to six months, but some produce lasting foveal defects. Reviews and case reports also link repeated bright-light exposure to concerns about macular degeneration.

angle.text: Some users look at the sun hoping for lighter iris colour, sharper vision and a mood lift through light exposure to the eyes. The practice dates to early 20th-century eye exercises, and ophthalmology literature documents retinal burns from direct sun viewing.

lead: Sungazing is the practice of looking directly at the sun, often near dawn or dusk, as a spiritual or health practice. A general reference describes it as an unsafe and pseudoscientific practice; it was promoted in the early 20th century by William Horatio Bates under the name sunning, as part of his eye exercises for myopia.[1]

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve eyesight, mood, skin or eye colour, with some users posting about their own experiences, including floaters.[2] No published trial has tested these claims. The medical literature instead documents solar retinopathy, a retinal injury following exposure to the sun's light, including from direct sungazing.[3][4]

paras: Bates promoted sunning as part of a set of eye exercises in the early 20th century, and it became a popular alternative therapy; the methods were later criticised for lacking scientific rigour.[1] A 1967 British Medical Journal report stated that Bates advocated prolonged sungazing as treatment for myopia with disastrous results.[1] The practice also exists in religious and spiritual traditions, typically at sunrise or sunset.[1]

A 2024 literature review describes solar retinopathy as retinal injury from unprotected excessive light exposure, associated with direct sungazing, sunbathing, laser pointers and welding arcs. Symptoms are usually bilateral and include reduced vision, central or paracentral blind spots, distorted vision, light sensitivity and headache. Recovery commonly occurs spontaneously within weeks to six months.[3]

Case reports describe a young woman with bilateral central blind spots and distorted vision after one to two minutes of direct sungazing; yellow macular lesions and retinal pigment epithelial defects were seen on imaging, and she was managed conservatively.[5] A primary-care eye clinic series found macular lesions consistent with solar retinopathy in 0.14 percent of patients, with sungazing as the most common history, and generally good visual acuity.[6] Imaging studies describe characteristic partial-thickness holes in the outer retina at the fovea in chronic cases.[7]

A 1988 review concluded that high-energy visible and ultraviolet photons can cause photochemical damage to retinal molecules, with oxygen-driven free-radical effects, and that this damage falls in the same region that degenerates in age-related macular degeneration.[8] A 2022 perspective on the so-called blue light hazard notes that blue light is highly toxic to the retina in brief abnormally intense exposures such as sungazing, but argues that ordinary environmental light exposure is not shown to cause such damage.[9]
A 1993 study documented the ultrastructural changes in a patient who agreed to stare at the sun before eye removal for a choroidal tumour, describing damage to cone and rod outer segments.[10]

No studies found testing sungazing for eyesight, mood, skin or appearance benefits. The published human literature consists of case reports, case series and imaging studies of injury, including solar retinopathy after sungazing and solar eclipse viewing.[3][5][6][7]

On looksmax.org, one user described sungazing for one to two hours a day for a month and said he could perceive his surroundings through closed eyelids, and also reported floaters from earlier practice; another user in the thread asked what benefit that would be.[2] Some users have discussed whether it could lighten iris colour, while others have warned of eye damage.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, sungazing is discussed by a few users as an experiment for eyesight, vision and eye colour, with other members expressing concern about eye damage.[2]

claims.claim: Sungazing lets you see through closed eyelids and improves vision.
Sun exposure to the iris could lighten eye colour.

timeline.event: Bates advocates prolonged sungazing for myopia, per a 1967 BMJ report.[1]
A short British Medical Journal piece on sungazing appears.[11]
Ultrastructural findings in solar retinopathy after deliberate sungazing are published.[10]
A literature review summarises pathogenesis and management of solar retinopathy.[3]
